title: How Not to Launch an AI-Powered Product
summary: Useful technology still has to be usable. I defined the user requirements for an AI assistant, then tracked what happened when they were cut from the launch.
role: Senior individual contributor leading experience research and scoping
collaboration: Service design and an applied AI specialist.
outcome: Leadership removed the user requirements to ship within the available resources and technical capabilities. Tracking reached launch. Customer engagement fell after early interest, and internal adoption stayed low.

blocks.text: The technology was useful. People still struggled to use it.

I led experience research and scoping for one internally built assistant with two deployments. Customers encountered it on the public site. Service and account-management representatives used it inside their working console.
Leadership removed the user requirements from the launch scope, prioritizing speed to market within the resources and technical capabilities available.

I specified how the assistant should handle uncertainty, waiting and failure, and what representatives needed before sending a reply. The demonstrations below show those requirements, all removed from launch.
An answer it should never have given
In testing, we asked for an account balance. The assistant returned a specific figure with supporting detail. The required response was a referral to an account manager.
I traced the answer to a sample account statement in the source documentation. The warehouse contained an example of the precise thing the assistant was not supposed to produce.
I required a referral to an account manager for this kind of question. That requirement was removed from the launch scope.
Requirements for waiting and failure
This assistant stood in for the opening minutes of a service conversation. It had to remain courteous and helpful, including when it failed.
I specified acknowledgment between 0.1 and 0.4 seconds. At three seconds, a holding message. At seven, thanks for waiting and an apology.

At ten seconds, or immediately on a stall or critical error, the assistant had to say it could not answer and offer a route to help. A related article, the correct support channel, or an account manager. The person should not have to keep rephrasing a question the system had already lost.
Those timings were project requirements. They describe the experience I specified, not a universal limit on human patience or a measured production response time.
Waiting messages, help routes, streaming and follow-up questions were part of the user requirements. None reached launch.
Requirements for the representative

Representatives needed the conversation history, a summary of what had been tried, and references beside the draft. I also specified compliance alerts and nudges when a reply might be incorrect, while the representative could still change it. Leadership removed these requirements, including the review controls, from the launch scope.
Those requirements put assistance around the conversation. The representative retained responsibility for the response.
The launch decision and the result
I secured tracking on the customer-facing assistant before launch. It let us see whether people kept using what we shipped.

Customers found it and used it. Engagement then fell away, with the decline correlated with response speed and interaction friction. Internal adoption stayed low, with representatives citing accuracy and waiting.
The record does not isolate the effect of each feature, and it supplies no numerical uplift to claim. It does show that initial interest was not enough to sustain use.

My lesson from the failure: removing these requirements left people to manage the wait, judge the answer and find help themselves. The technology's usefulness could not make up for the difficulty of using it.
No matter how valuable something is, if it is not usable, it is not used.
